title: Composite Indexes: Column Order, Leftmost Prefix, and Covering Indexes
description: Composite Indexes: Column Order, Leftmost Prefix, and Covering Indexes. Interview-first coverage of mechanisms, prediction, diagnosis, and trade-offs.
learningObjectives: Choose composite index order from predicates and ordering.
Explain leading-column behavior without overstating it.
Distinguish key columns from INCLUDE payload.
Diagnose why an index does not fit a query.

mentalModel.text: A composite index is a lookup list sorted by several columns in order. For an index on (tenant_id, status, created_at), rows are grouped by tenant first, then by status within each tenant, and then by time. That order determines which queries can jump to a narrow range and which must scan much more of the index.

blocks.text: A composite index sorts by its first column, then by its second column within equal first-column values, and so on.

For an index on (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC), tenant_id is sorted first, status is sorted within each tenant, and time is sorted within each tenant/status pair. This is why column order changes what the index can find efficiently.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE INDEX events_tenant_status_created_idx ON events (tenant_id,status,created_at DESC);

blocks.title: What column order changes
rows: Find one tenant, then narrow by status and time.
A query filtering only by status cannot usually jump to one narrow range.
Fetch one tenant's newest rows in order; LIMIT may stop early.
Does not directly provide one global newest-first list across all tenants.
Store status in the index to help return it without a table lookup when visibility permits.
Included columns do not change search order and make the index larger.

blocks.problem: You create an index on (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC).
reasoning: Rows are ordered first by tenant_id.
Within each tenant, rows are ordered by status.
Within each tenant/status pair, rows are ordered by newest created_at first.
blocks.outcome: The order lets PostgreSQL narrow by leading columns and may provide a requested sort, but it is not a shortcut for every filter combination.

blocks.text: Put index columns in an order that supports the queries you actually run. Equality filters on leading columns often narrow the search before a range or ordering column.

Put the columns used to narrow the search first, based on the actual query. Equality filters on leading columns often narrow the search well. A range filter can limit how much later columns help; ORDER BY and LIMIT can also make one order much better than another.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: SELECT id,created_at FROM events WHERE tenant_id=7 AND status='open' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

steps.title: Identify query shape
steps.description: Write down predicates, joins, ordering, limit, and selected columns.

steps.title: Predict the mechanism
steps.description: Explain which pages, entries, or operators the database is likely to visit.

steps.title: Validate the plan
steps.description: Use actual rows and buffers to compare prediction with observed work.

blocks.problem: A feed query filters by tenant_id, sorts newest first, and returns 20 rows.
reasoning: An index on (tenant_id, created_at DESC) can seek to one tenant and read its newest entries in order.
An index starting with created_at may not narrow to that tenant as directly.
If the query filters only by status, an index whose first column is tenant_id may not provide a narrow lookup by status alone.
blocks.outcome: Design from WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY, and LIMIT together; column order determines which parts of the query an index can support.

reasoning: The query filters on `tenant_id = 7` and `status = 'open'`; these equality predicates define the group to search.
Within that group, the result needs `created_at DESC`, so place the ordering column after the equality columns.

An index on `(tenant_id, status, created_at DESC)` can seek to that tenant/status range and read newest-first. An index on `(created_at DESC, tenant_id, status)` orders by time across all tenants first, so it may have to examine many entries before finding 20 rows for tenant 7.
blocks.outcome: Leading columns determine which contiguous part of the index can be searched directly. Column order should match the query's filters and required order.
blocks.problem: You need the latest 20 open events for tenant 7.

blocks.text: A covering index contains all columns needed by a query. PostgreSQL's INCLUDE adds output columns without making them part of the search order.

A covering index stores all the values a query needs, either as searchable key columns or as included payload. In PostgreSQL, INCLUDE columns can supply output values but do not change the index's sort order. More stored values mean a larger index and more write work.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE INDEX events_tenant_created_cover_idx ON events (tenant_id,created_at DESC) INCLUDE (event_type,actor_id);

blocks.problem: A feed query returns tenant_id, created_at, and status.
reasoning: Use `tenant_id` and `created_at` as key columns to support filtering and ordering.
If the query also returns `event_type`, include that column in the index payload so PostgreSQL may return it without fetching the heap row.
The index grows larger and updates to included values require index maintenance. Even when all columns are present, PostgreSQL may still visit the heap to check row visibility.
blocks.outcome: INCLUDE can reduce row fetches, but measure the read benefit against index size and write overhead.

blocks.text: When an index provides the requested order, PostgreSQL may avoid a separate sort. LIMIT can make this especially useful because the scan can stop early.

If the index order matches a query's ORDER BY, PostgreSQL may return rows already sorted and avoid a separate Sort step. With LIMIT, it may stop once it has found enough rows, rather than sorting every matching row first.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created_idx ON orders (customer_id,created_at DESC,id DESC);

blocks.prompt: Does the existence of an index guarantee PostgreSQL will use it?
blocks.explanation: The planner compares estimated costs, and another access path may be cheaper.

blocks.problem: Return the newest 20 orders for customer 42.
reasoning: An index on (customer_id, created_at DESC) can locate customer 42's range.
The entries already arrive newest first, so PostgreSQL may stop after finding 20 qualifying rows.
If the index order does not match the requested order, a separate Sort may be needed.
blocks.outcome: An index can save both lookup work and sorting work when its order matches the query.

blocks.text: When an index is not helping, compare the query shape with the index definition before adding another index.

To diagnose an index that isn't helping, write down the query's WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY, LIMIT, and selected columns. Compare that shape with the index's column order, then inspect the actual plan to see how many rows and table pages it reads.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id,created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id=42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;

blocks.problem: An index exists on (tenant_id, status, created_at), but a query filters only by status.
reasoning: The index is sorted by tenant_id first, so rows with the same status may be spread across many tenant ranges.
Check whether another index would serve a frequent workload well enough to justify its storage and write cost.
Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to verify the access path and number of rows/pages touched.
blocks.outcome: Index design is about matching real predicates and ordering, not merely including every column mentioned in the query.

blocks.text: ### The right index for one query can be wrong for another

blocks.title: A global feed does not filter by tenant
blocks.source:
SELECT id, created_at
FROM events
WHERE created_at >= now() - interval '1 day'
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 50;

blocks.title: Two real query shapes
rows: One tenant's newest events: `WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50`
The leading equality key narrows to one tenant and the remaining keys provide order.
Newest events globally across all tenants
`(created_at DESC, id DESC)` (test against the workload)
The tenant-leading index groups entries by tenant; without a tenant predicate it cannot directly provide one global newest-first range.

blocks.text: Do not build both automatically. A second index costs disk, cache capacity, write maintenance and vacuum work. Compare the importance/frequency of each query, selectivity, actual plans, and write load before deciding whether one or both access paths deserve an index.

1. Problem and motivation — A feed filters by tenant, sorts newest-first, and returns 20 rows. Both candidate indexes contain the right columns, but their leading keys determine how much work the database may need to do.

2. Definition and design choice — A composite B-tree is ordered by the first key, then by the next key within equal first-key values. Equality predicates, range predicates, ordering, and LIMIT determine which column order is useful.

steps.description: A composite index sorts by its first column, then by its second column within equal first-column values, and so on.

steps.title: Choosing order
steps.description: Put index columns in an order that supports the queries you actually run. Equality filters on leading columns often narrow the search before a range or ordering column.

steps.description: When an index provides the requested order, PostgreSQL may avoid a separate sort. LIMIT can make this especially useful because the scan can stop early.

blocks.problem: For `WHERE tenant_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`, compare `(created_at, tenant_id)` and `(tenant_id, created_at DESC)`.
reasoning: The tenant-first index can seek to tenant 7 and read its rows in timestamp order, often stopping after 20 rows.
The timestamp-first index is ordered globally by time, not by tenant. It may inspect many rows belonging to other tenants before finding 20 matches.
INCLUDE can store projected columns in the index, but increases index size and write work and does not guarantee an index-only scan.
blocks.outcome: Design around actual predicates, ordering, LIMIT, and projected columns, then check actual rows and buffers in the plan.

blocks.title: 5. Anti-pattern to avoid
blocks.content: Column order is a workload decision: consider equality/range predicates, ordering, joins, LIMIT, overlapping indexes, and write cost.

blocks.prompt: 6. Interview probe — An index exists on (tenant_id, created_at DESC). A tenant feed runs `WHERE tenant_id = 7 AND created_at >= DATE '2026-10-01' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`. Why is this index a strong candidate?
blocks.answer: The key order matches the equality filter followed by the range/order requirement. Whether the final plan uses it still depends on costs, statistics, and selected columns.
blocks.explanation: A strong answer connects the problem to the mechanism, states assumptions and trade-offs, and explains how to verify the decision in practice.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Trade-off 1
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Column order is a workload decision: consider equality/range predicates, ordering, joins, LIMIT, overlapping indexes, and write cost.

revisionSheet.text: Leading equality keys often define the narrowest range.
Compatible key order can satisfy ORDER BY and allow early stop for LIMIT.
INCLUDE payload can cover output but does not affect key order.
Validate with actual plans and workload measurements.

questions.prompt: An index exists on (tenant_id, created_at DESC). A tenant feed runs `WHERE tenant_id = 7 AND created_at >= DATE '2026-10-01' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`. Why is this index a strong candidate?

options.text: The equality on the leading key narrows the tenant, and the next key can support the time range and order.
The index is useful only if tenant_id is the most selective column in every tenant's data.
The index guarantees an index-only scan even when the query selects columns not stored in it.
The index makes created_at globally ordered across all tenants, so tenant_id is irrelevant.

questions.explanation: The key order matches the equality filter followed by the range/order requirement. Whether the final plan uses it still depends on costs, statistics, and selected columns.

questions.prompt: What is the key-order principle for (a,b,c)?

options.text: Sort by a, then b within a, then c within a and b
The most selective column is automatically first

questions.prompt: Why can a range predicate on a leading key limit later-key narrowing?

options.text: It scans a range of leading values, so later keys may not form one narrow contiguous global range
PostgreSQL always ignores keys after the first

questions.explanation: Later keys may still help filter or order, but may not narrow the initial range as well.

questions.prompt: Why put tenant_id first for a tenant feed?

options.text: The query fixes tenant_id and needs that tenant's rows in time order
It is always most selective in every dataset

questions.explanation: Design for actual query patterns, not a universal selectivity rule.

options.text: Adds non-key payload that may cover output without changing key order

questions.explanation: INCLUDE stores payload, not search-order keys.

questions.prompt: What is the concern with (created_at, tenant_id) for one tenant's feed?

options.text: It may scan many timestamps across tenants before filtering the target tenant

questions.explanation: Tenant-first indexing usually narrows this query more directly.

questions.prompt: Why can a matching index help ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10?

options.text: It may produce rows in the needed order and stop early

questions.explanation: A compatible ordered path can avoid a separate sort and stop after enough rows.

questions.prompt: A query filters by `created_at >= now() - interval '1 day'` and sorts by `created_at DESC`. An existing index is `(tenant_id, created_at DESC)`, and EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan. What is the most defensible diagnosis?

options.text: The query lacks a constraint on the leading tenant_id key, so the index may not provide a narrow global range; compare a created_at-leading index against the workload.
PostgreSQL never uses composite indexes when a query has ORDER BY.
The index is corrupt because all indexes must be used whenever a column appears in the predicate.
Add created_at as an INCLUDE column to make it the first ordering key.

questions.explanation: The existing key order is tenant-first. A created_at-leading index may fit this query better, but validate selectivity, plans, and write/storage costs before adding it.

questions.prompt: Which factors should inform composite index design?

options.text: Only highest-cardinality column regardless of workload

questions.explanation: Design balances filtering, ordering, joins, coverage, and costs.

questions.prompt: Which are limits/costs of covering indexes?

options.text: Visibility map can still require heap fetches

questions.explanation: Coverage is conditional and costs storage/write work.

questions.prompt: An index on (a,b) is always as effective for WHERE b = ? as an index on (b).
questions.explanation: Leading-key order matters; skip scan is conditional.

questions.prompt: INCLUDE columns participate in B-tree search ordering just like key columns.
questions.explanation: INCLUDE columns are payload, not ordering keys.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A multi-tenant API runs WHERE tenant_id=? AND status=? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Propose an index and validation plan.
strongAnswerPoints: Consider (tenant_id,status,created_at DESC) if predicates are common.
Compare with tenant/time feed queries and existing prefixes.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: A candidate is (tenant_id,status,created_at DESC) if both equality predicates are common. If tenant-only recent-feed queries dominate, (tenant_id,created_at DESC) may be more reusable. Compare representative plans and write costs.

interviewScenarios.prompt: An index on (account_id,created_at) exists, but a query filters only by created_at. Explain.
strongAnswerPoints: The leading account_id means created_at-only filtering may not be one narrow contiguous range.
Skip scan can apply in some cases, not all.
Check EXPLAIN and compare a created_at-leading index against workload cost.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: The index is ordered by account first. A created_at-only predicate normally cannot seek directly to one contiguous range across all accounts. Skip scan is conditional; validate the plan and workload before adding another index.
